transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nadar (Redwood SE), Marta Silva (HelixCare Head of ML), Daniel O'Connor (HelixCare Platform Eng), Liam Park (HelixCare SRE)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on integrating HelixCare's customer scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness. Primary concerns: streaming vs non-streaming behavior, realistic load shaping from production traces, success criteria (latency, p99, throughput), and timeline for a controlled benchmark run. Some minor transcription artifacts in places.

Topics: benchmark planning, harness integration, workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming, success criteria, timelines

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm an AE, with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta Silva: Doing well, thanks. We've been talking internally about coming up with a proper benchmark for the POC. Want to make sure it's representative of our e2e pipeline.
[00:15] Priya Nadar: Great, hi Marta — quick note, we'll want both a non-streaming and a streaming workload because your app uses streaming for user-facing sessions but also batch scoring for backfill.
[00:28] Daniel O'Connor: Yeah, exactly. Most of our traffic is streaming for interactive sessions — low latency, incremental tokens. Backfill jobs are long sequences but can be non-streamed.
[00:38] Jordan Lee: Cool. For success criteria what have you been thinking? Typical things are p50/p95/p99 latency targets for interactive, throughput for batch, and cost per 1k inferences.
[00:49] Marta Silva: We're aiming for p99 < 1s for interactive at our usual concurrency — which is, ish, 120 concurrent sessions in peak. For batch, we want at least X throughput, I'll try not to use variables, but approx 500 sequences/hour per worker.
[01:05] Priya Nadar: Good baseline. Two clarifications: 1) when you say p99 < 1s is that token-level or full-response? 2) What's your typical avg sequence length and long-tail? That drives KV cache and memory sizing.
[01:18] Marta Silva: That's full-response for interactive; average sequence length around 180 tokens, long-tail up to 2k for some transcripts. We'll pull histograms.
[01:27] Daniel O'Connor: Also we need to validate memory footprint on a 48GB GPU for quantized variants — so quantization profiles matter.
[01:36] Priya Nadar: Noted. For the harness integration, Jordan, maybe you want to run through our typical approach?
[01:41] Jordan Lee: Sure. Redwood's benchmark harness can ingest customer scripts — either our simple JSON request traces or your own driver (we support Python scripts that call our REST/streaming endpoints, or a gRPC harness). The usual pattern: 1) replay production traces with preserved inter-arrival times for interactive; 2) run synthetic sustained throughput tests for batch; 3) measure p50/p95/p99, GPU util, latency tail, token/sec, and cost telemetry.
[02:07] Marta Silva: When you say "ingest scripts" — is that a blackbox runner or do we need to rewrite our client code? We have a custom connector.
[02:14] Priya Nadar: You can drop in your script; our harness exposes a small shim. Two options: run your script unchanged behind our shim (we forward traffic) or adapt it to use the harness client library. The shim has been stable but in some cases you need small edits to handle streaming chunk boundaries.
[02:29] Daniel O'Connor: For streaming, we use websockets in prod. Does your harness support websockets? And can it do long-lived connections across many sessions?
[02:36] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support streaming via WebSocket and HTTP chunked transfer; we can simulate long-lived connections and maintain many concurrent connections. The only caveat is that some open-source load tools don't work well with streaming, so we recommend our harness for streaming tests.
[02:51] Liam Park: What's the recommended load generator for non-streaming? We currently use wrk and a mix of locust for some flows.
[02:57] Priya Nadar: For REST non-streaming we often use locust or Vegeta for request shaping; wrk is fine but less flexible for complex payloads. For batch throughput we use a custom parallel runner that posts at configured concurrency and collects token-level metrics.
[03:13] Jordan Lee: We'll provide a sample market harness repo and a small Python example that wraps your existing connector. Link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmark-harness (demo link, we'll share real in email).
[03:24] Marta Silva: Awesome. Now about workload sizing — we can provide a 24h trace of production requests with timestamps, sequence lengths, and whether the sessions were streaming or not. You said the harness can preserve inter-arrival timings?
[03:36] Priya Nadar: Yes. We have a trace replay mode that honors timestamps and simulates the same concurrency profile; that helps find real-world hotspots and queueing effects.
[03:45] Daniel O'Connor: For the POC, do we need dedicated hardware or can we validate on Redwood hosted? We prefer dedicated for more predictable SLOs.
[03:53] Jordan Lee: For the most accurate p99 latency and tail behavior we recommend dedicated capacity so there's no noisy neighbor effect. But initial smoke and functional tests can run on hosted to validate harness integration.
[04:05] Marta Silva: Cost piece — how do you measure cost per inference? We want a number we can plug into our TCO model.
[04:12] Priya Nadar: We report tokens-per-second and tokens-per-dollar using the committed price for dedicated or the hosted per-token. For the POC we'll run identical workloads across variants (fp16, 8-bit quant) and show delta in cost and latency.
[04:24] Jordan Lee: Also we'll surface batching and KV cache hit rates; sometimes a high cache hit rate drastically lowers token compute.
[04:31] Marta Silva: Good. Streaming vs non-streaming differences — is resource usage different?
[04:36] Priya Nadar: Streaming keeps long-lived sessions and requires connection handling and memory for KV caches across the session. For many short messages it's CPU/network bound. Non-streaming lets the runtime free per-request state sooner which can increase throughput for batch. So both need to be measured.
[04:51] Daniel O'Connor: For the streaming run, we want to test both many short sessions and fewer long sessions. Can the harness param those?
[04:57] Jordan Lee: Yes we can param: concurrency, session length distribution, token arrival rates. We'll work with your trace or generate synthetic mixes.
[05:06] Marta Silva: Regarding metrics to collect, besides latency and throughput, we want GPU mem, GPU util, NVLink stats if possible, and per-request logs to trace regressions.
[05:16] Priya Nadar: We capture GPU util and memory, and can integrate with your monitoring via metrics exporter. We also provide request-level ids so you can correlate with your logs.
[05:26] Jordan Lee: A practical note: for streaming tests please ensure the client script sends incremental partials like prod; we sometimes see differences when clients batch partials.
[05:36] Marta Silva: Understood. We'll add partials in the sample trace.
[05:40] [Speaker 1]: (crosstalk) yeah i think that's fine — little transcription glitch here
[05:45] Daniel O'Connor: Timeline question — how long does integration usually take? We're aiming for a one-week integration, one-week run/analysis, then decision.
[05:53] Priya Nadar: Typical: 3-5 business days to wire up traces and scripts and validate harness on a smoke test; then 2-3 days for the main run including a couple repeats for different model variants. So your 2-week window is reasonable.
[06:08] Marta Silva: Great. Any pitfalls you've seen?
[06:11] Jordan Lee: A few: 1) mismatched request shaping (burstiness vs constant rate) can produce misleading p99s; 2) streaming not simulated correctly by stateless load tools; 3) forgetting to run cold-start to warm KV caches before measuring; 4) differences in tokenization between local and harness tokenizers.
[06:28] Daniel O'Connor: For cold starts — how do we warm caches?
[06:31] Priya Nadar: We run a warm-up phase that replays a fraction of traffic until KV hit rates stabilize. We'll include that step in the runbook.
[06:39] Marta Silva: On the security side, we'll need audit logs and SSO for the test env. Any issues?
[06:45] Jordan Lee: For dedicated POC we can set up temporary SSO or we can provide scoped API keys. Audit logs are captured and can be exported. We'll share the security docs as part of the follow-up.
[06:56] Liam Park: For the infra, we may need a test VPC peering or egress rules to let the harness reach our staging endpoints.
[07:02] Priya Nadar: We'll give specific network requirements; usually outbound HTTPS/WebSocket and a small set of ports.
[07:09] Marta Silva: Anything else on metrics?
[07:11] Jordan Lee: We'll also present a regression diff tool that compares runs across model variants and highlights latency/cost tradeoffs.
[07:17] Daniel O'Connor: Good to see that.
[07:19] Jordan Lee: Ok, recap / next steps: we'll email the benchmark harness repo and the runbook, Priya will add the streaming config, Marta/Daniel will provide traces and provisioning details, and we'll schedule the run for week of 12/14.
[07:34] Marta Silva: Sounds good. Thanks.
[07:36] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and action items in the next 24-48h.
[07:42] [end of recording]
